primary_claim: Natural Language Autoencoders (NLAs) — a pair of jointly RL-trained LLMs (an activation verbalizer and activation reconstructor) that translate residual stream activations into natural-language text and back — produce explanations that grow more informative over training and surface unverbalized evaluation awareness in Claude Opus 4.6 (e.g. evaluation-awareness signs in 16% of a destructive-coding-action test and 26% of SWE-bench Verified problems, vs <1% on opted-in real claude.ai usage), and NLA-equipped auditors uncover a target model's hidden misaligned motivation 12-15% of the time without training-data access versus <3% without NLAs.

effect.metric: rate of NLA-detected evaluation awareness on transcripts; auditing-game win rate
effect.value: 16% NLA-detected eval awareness on destructive-coding-action test, 26% on SWE-bench Verified, <1% on real opted-in claude.ai usage; NLA-equipped auditors win 12-15% of the time vs <3% without NLAs

contradicts_or_qualifies: reliance on verbalized eval awareness alone (e.g. in the companion post on Fortress), since NLAs show models can suspect evaluation without saying so
stated_future_work: make NLAs cheaper and more reliable
continue using NLAs in future pre-deployment alignment audits
further develop the general class of techniques for producing human-readable text explanations of model activations
limitations_stated: NLA explanations can be wrong, including verifiable factual hallucinations (inventing details not in the transcript)
claims about internal reasoning are harder to verify than factual hallucinations

NLAs are expensive: training requires RL on two model copies, and inference generates hundreds of tokens per activation, making them impractical for monitoring every token of long transcripts or for large-scale training-time monitoring
auditing game is a toy model of misalignment, so results should be read cautiously
quote: An auditor equipped with NLAs successfully uncovered the target model's hidden motivation between 12% and 15% of the time, even without access to the training data that implanted it. Without NLAs, the auditor won less than 3% of the time, even when provided other interpretability tools.
